title: Cracking, Reforming and Gasoline Quality
notes: **Cracking definition:** Breaking down long-chain hydrocarbons into smaller, more useful molecules. Crude oil contains many long-chain fractions that are less valuable than short-chain ones used as fuels.

**Thermal cracking:** High temperature (750-900°C) and high pressure (7-50 atm) breaks C-C bonds homolytically, producing a mixture of alkanes and alkenes via free radical mechanism. Example: $C_{10}H_{22} \xrightarrow{750^\circ C} C_5H_{12} + C_5H_{10}$.

**Catalytic cracking:** Lower temperature (450-500°C) using silica-alumina zeolite catalyst. Produces branched-chain alkanes and aromatic compounds, which have higher octane numbers. Favored for gasoline production.
**Steam cracking:** Hydrocarbons are mixed with steam and heated to 850°C. Used primarily to produce ethylene ($C_2H_4$) and propylene ($C_3H_6$), which are raw materials for plastics and polymers.

**Reforming definition:** Conversion of straight-chain alkanes into branched-chain alkanes and aromatic hydrocarbons using platinum on alumina ($Pt/Al_2O_3$) catalyst at 500°C and high pressure. Example: n-hexane → cyclohexane → benzene.

**Octane number:** A measure of the antiknock quality of gasoline. The reference fuels are iso-octane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane) = 100 and n-heptane = 0. A fuel with octane number 90 knocks like a mixture of 90% iso-octane and 10% n-heptane.
**Knocking:** Premature auto-ignition of fuel-air mixture before the spark fires, causing engine damage and reduced efficiency. High compression ratio engines require higher octane fuels.

**Cetane number:** Measure of the ignition quality of diesel fuel. n-cetane ($C_{16}H_{34}$) = 100 and 2,2,4,4,6,8,8-heptamethylnonane = 15. Higher cetane number means shorter ignition delay and smoother diesel combustion. Ideal: 40-55.

**Why octane and cetane are opposites:** Branched alkanes have high octane (resist auto-ignition) but low cetane (slow to ignite when needed). Linear alkanes have low octane but high cetane. This is why gasoline and diesel require different hydrocarbon profiles.

**Lead-free gasoline additives:** Methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE, $C_5H_{12}O$) raises octane and adds oxygen. Ethanol ($C_2H_5OH$) is a renewable octane booster. Benzene and toluene are aromatic octane enhancers but are regulated due to toxicity.

**Tetraethyl lead (TEL):** $Pb(C_2H_5)_4$ was the most effective antiknock agent, boosting octane by 10-15 points. Banned in most countries due to lead poisoning — lead damages the catalytic converter and causes neurotoxicity.
**Industrial importance:** Catalytic cracking converts ~45% of crude oil into gasoline. Without cracking, only ~20% of crude oil would yield useful gasoline fractions.
confusion: **Cracking and reforming are the same process** — Cracking breaks long-chain hydrocarbons into smaller ones (decreasing molecular weight), while reforming rearranges the molecular structure (isomerization, cyclization, aromatization) without significantly changing molecular weight.

**Higher octane number means more energy content** — Octane number measures resistance to knocking, not energy density. In fact, n-heptane (octane = 0) has slightly higher energy density than iso-octane (octane = 100). High octane allows higher compression ratios, which extract more energy.

**Cetane number and octane number work the same way** — They are essentially inversely related. Diesel engines need fuel that ignites easily (high cetane), while petrol engines need fuel that resists auto-ignition (high octane). A high-octane fuel would be terrible diesel fuel.

universalFacts: Approximately 45% of every barrel of crude oil is processed through catalytic cracking to produce gasoline — it is the single most important process in petroleum refining.
Banned worldwide since the 2000s, tetraethyl lead once caused widespread lead contamination — blood lead levels in urban populations dropped dramatically after leaded gasoline was phased out.
Modern catalytic reforming uses bimetallic catalysts (Pt-Re or Pt-Sn on alumina) that are about 10 times more active than early platinum-only catalysts.
MTBE was once the primary octane booster but was banned in many US states after it was found to contaminate groundwater due to its high water solubility.
The octane rating printed at petrol pumps (e.g., 95 RON, 98 RON) represents the Research Octane Number, measured under controlled engine conditions at 600 rpm.
